land-ethic: The land ethic, articulated by the American forester and conservationist Aldo Leopold in A Sand County Almanac (1949), proposes that ethical concern should extend beyond individual humans to the whole biotic community of soils, waters, plants, and animals. Leopold famously held that a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of that community, and wrong when it tends otherwise. It reframes humans not as conquerors of the natural world but as plain members and citizens of it, responding to the destructive effects of treating land purely as economic property.
deep-ecology: Deep ecology, a term coined by the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess in the early 1970s, contrasts a superficial environmentalism concerned with pollution and resource management against a deeper view that questions the underlying worldview placing humans above nature. It affirms the intrinsic value of all living things, independent of their usefulness to people, and calls for a fundamental shift toward ecological self-realization and a smaller human footprint. The movement responds to the sense that piecemeal reform cannot address the root causes of environmental crisis.
ecofeminism: Ecofeminism examines the connection between the domination of women and the domination of nature, arguing that both stem from a shared logic of hierarchy and dualism that ranks culture over nature, reason over emotion, and man over woman. The Australian philosopher Val Plumwood, among its leading theorists, criticized the way Western thought treats nature as a passive, valueless background to human activity. The view seeks to dismantle these interlocking structures of oppression and to recover a relational understanding of humans as embedded in the natural world.
animal-rights: The subjects-of-a-life account of animal rights, developed by the American philosopher Tom Regan in The Case for Animal Rights (1983), holds that many animals are not mere resources but conscious beings with beliefs, desires, memory, and a welfare that matters to them. Because such creatures are subjects of a life, Regan argues, they possess inherent value and a right not to be harmed or used merely as means to human ends. This deontological position differs from utilitarian animal ethics by grounding protection in rights rather than in the calculation of overall pleasure and pain.
climate-ethics: Climate ethics is the branch of moral philosophy that studies the ethical questions raised by human-caused climate change, including who bears responsibility for emissions, how burdens and benefits should be fairly distributed, and what is owed to future generations and to the world's poorest people. It grapples with problems of collective action, historical responsibility, and the difficulty of assigning duties when harms are diffuse and long-delayed. The field asks how principles of justice apply when the consequences of present choices fall largely on those who did least to cause them.
anthropocentrism: Anthropocentrism is the view that human beings are the central or most significant entities in the world, and that value or moral standing belongs primarily or exclusively to them. In environmental philosophy the term often carries a critical edge, naming the assumption that nature matters only insofar as it serves human interests. Critics argue that this outlook licenses exploitation of the nonhuman world, while defenders distinguish a chauvinistic version from a more modest claim that humans can only evaluate the world from a human standpoint.
food-ethics: Food ethics is the study of the moral questions surrounding how food is produced, distributed, and consumed, spanning the treatment of animals in agriculture, the environmental impact of farming, fair labor and trade, and personal choices such as vegetarianism. It asks whether practices like factory farming are justifiable, how responsibility for hunger and food waste should be understood, and what a just food system would look like. The field connects individual eating habits to large-scale ethical, ecological, and economic concerns.
wilderness-ethics: Wilderness and nature aesthetics concern the value we find in wild places and the appropriate way to appreciate natural beauty. Ethically, debates turn on whether wilderness has worth apart from human use and whether the very idea of pristine, untouched nature is coherent given human history. Aesthetically, philosophers ask how appreciation of a landscape differs from appreciation of art, and whether knowledge of ecology and natural science should inform and deepen our experience of the natural world.
watchmaker-argument: The watchmaker argument, given its most famous form by the English clergyman William Paley in Natural Theology (1802), reasons that just as finding a watch on a heath would lead one to infer a designer, the intricate order and apparent purpose of living things point to an intelligent designer of nature. It is a version of the teleological, or design, argument for the existence of God. The argument was influentially challenged by David Hume before Paley and later undercut by Darwin's account of how natural selection can produce apparent design without a designer.
problem-of-evil: The problem of evil is the challenge of reconciling the existence of a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing, and wholly good with the reality of suffering and wrongdoing in the world. In its logical form it alleges an outright contradiction between such a God and any evil at all, while its evidential form argues that the sheer amount and distribution of suffering makes God's existence unlikely. Responses, known as theodicies, appeal to free will, soul-making, or the limits of human understanding to explain why a good God might permit evil.
faith-vs-reason: The relationship between faith and reason concerns how religious belief stands in relation to rational argument and evidence. Positions range from rationalism, which holds that belief must be justified by reason, to fideism, which maintains that faith is independent of or even opposed to rational proof, with many thinkers seeking a middle path in which faith and reason are complementary. The debate runs throughout the history of philosophy and theology, from medieval attempts to demonstrate God's existence to modern discussions of whether religious commitment can be reasonable without conclusive proof.
meaning-of-life: The question of the meaning of life asks whether human existence has a point, purpose, or significance, and if so, what makes a life meaningful. Answers divide between those who locate meaning in something beyond us, such as God or an objective moral order, and those who hold that meaning is created by human beings through their projects, relationships, and values. The question gained special urgency in modern thought as traditional religious frameworks were questioned, prompting responses ranging from nihilism to existentialist affirmations of self-created purpose.
immortality: Questions of immortality and the soul concern whether some part of a person, often called the soul or mind, survives bodily death, and what such survival would consist in. Dualist traditions, from Plato onward, treat the soul as a distinct immaterial substance capable of existing apart from the body, while materialists deny any such separable entity and tie personal existence to the living organism. The topic bears on religious hopes for an afterlife, on debates about personal identity over time, and on what it would even mean for the same person to persist beyond death.
i-thou: The I–Thou relation is a central idea of the Austrian-born Jewish philosopher Martin Buber, set out in his 1923 work I and Thou. Buber distinguishes two basic ways of relating to the world: the I–It attitude, in which we treat others as objects to be used, analyzed, or experienced, and the I–Thou attitude, in which we meet another as a genuine presence in a direct, mutual encounter. Authentic existence, for Buber, is dialogical, arising in these moments of meeting, which he saw as ultimately pointing toward relation with the eternal Thou, or God.
tillich-ground-of-being: God as the ground of being is a conception developed by the German-American theologian Paul Tillich, who argued that God should not be thought of as a supreme entity existing alongside other things but as being-itself, the source and ground from which all existence derives. On this view, to call God a being among beings, however great, is to diminish the divine; God is instead the depth and ground of everything that is. Tillich linked this idea to faith understood as ultimate concern, an orientation toward what matters unconditionally in human life.
